title: The Cedar and the Ash: from the House of Ishtar at Uruk to the Burning of Solomon's Temple
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Uruk, Eanna: the boy made high priest of Ishtar
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no birth record survives. The estimate is derived from his holding the Eanna priesthood in 626/625 BC, not from the length of his reign, and other figures in circulation (c. 634, no earlier than c. 630) cannot be squared with that office
stops.campa: Nabopolassar has broken Assyria and made himself king in Babylon, and he sends his eldest son south to Uruk, to Eanna, the house of Ishtar, a precinct older than any dynasty that has ever governed it. The boy holds the office of sanga there from 626 or 625. That priesthood is how historians reach his birth at all: no tablet records the year, so they count back from the age a high priest must be. He learns grain rosters and ration lists and the language of dedication before he learns war, and he will use that language on his own bricks for forty years.
suggested_refs: The Eanna temple archive of Uruk, which fixes his priesthood to 626/625 BC
sources: Eanna temple and administrative archive texts

stops.name: Harran, the last Assyrian city taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Assyria is dying by pieces. Nineveh fell four years ago, and what remains of the empire has withdrawn to Harran under Ashur-uballit, propped up by Egyptian troops. Nabopolassar marches on the city with Median allies, and a contemporary letter puts the crown prince in the column. Harran belongs to Sin, the moon god, whose temple there will trouble Babylonian kings until the dynasty ends. Nebuchadnezzar takes it as a soldier under his father's command. Nobody yet calls him a builder.
suggested_refs: The temple of Sin at Harran, last seat of the Assyrian rump state
sources: Contemporary letter cited in Wikipedia, 'Nebuchadnezzar II'

stops.name: Carchemish, the crossing of the Euphrates
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not given in the Chronicle
stops.campa: At the ford where the Euphrates bends into Syria, Necho II of Egypt holds the crossing with the last Assyrian field army beside him. Nebuchadnezzar, commanding for his father, crosses the river and destroys them; the Chronicle says the survivors were overtaken in the district of Hamath and that not a man escaped to his own country. Egypt loses Syria in an afternoon and will not hold it again. Jeremiah dates a prophecy to this battle by name, against the army of Pharaoh Necho at the river Euphrates, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim.
suggested_refs: The Jerablus mound at Carchemish, on the Turkish-Syrian border

stops.name: Hamath, the pursuit down the Orontes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the campaign season
stops.campa: He does not let the beaten army reform. The pursuit runs south down the Orontes and catches Necho's remnant near Hamath, and the Chronicle closes the season with a line of pure administration: he conquered the whole of Hatti. Hatti is the scribes' word for everything from the Amanus to the Egyptian border, with Damascus and Tyre and Jerusalem inside it. The kinglets who paid Egypt last year now owe Babylon. The man who has just annexed the Levant is still, in the dating formulas, only the son of the king.
suggested_refs: The citadel mound of Hama on the Orontes

stops.name: The Egyptian frontier near Pelusium, the news from Babylon
stops.date_confidence: the Chronicle dates the arrival of the news to 8 Abu, late July 605 BC; the death itself was earlier that month. The pool's date of 16 August is impossible, falling after the accession
stops.campa: Word comes up the coast road that Nabopolassar is dead in Babylon. The Chronicle records only that the news reached the camp on the eighth of Abu, in late July; the camp itself is not named, and Pelusium marks no more than the traditional edge of the theatre he is operating in. Berossus, quoted by Josephus, says he leaves the war and the captives and the plunder to his officers and crosses the desert with a small escort. The empire has no designated heir sitting in the city. He intends to be in it first.
suggested_refs: The desert road from the Levant to Babylon, crossed in weeks by a small mounted escort

stops.name: Babylon, the Southern Palace: he sits on the throne
stops.date_confidence: attested; the accession falls on 15 August 605 BC and the formal coronation separately on 7 September. Sources that give 1 Elul as 7 September conflate the two
stops.campa: He reaches Babylon and sits on the throne, and the Chronicle gives the act one flat line. Fifteenth of August by the modern count; the formal coronation waits until the seventh of September, and his first regnal year does not begin until Nisan of the following spring, so the months between are counted as an accession year and belong to nobody's reckoning but the scribes'. He is roughly thirty-seven. He will hold this palace ground for forty-three years and rebuild the city around it in glazed brick.
suggested_refs: The Kasr mound at Babylon, site of the Southern Palace

stops.name: Ashkelon, the city turned into a ruin heap
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In his first full regnal year he turns into Philistia and destroys Ashkelon, a port that has refused submission. The Chronicle says he turned the city into a ruin heap and carried off its king. Excavation found the sentence intact in the ground: burned houses, a wine shop crushed under collapsed mudbrick, a destruction layer that dates to this winter and no other. Jeremiah hears of it in Jerusalem. Before the season closes, the Chronicle says, all the kings of Hatti come before him and he receives their heavy tribute.
suggested_refs: The 604 BC destruction layer at Tel Ashkelon, excavated by Lawrence Stager's expedition
sources: Ashkelon excavation reports (Stager), via summary literature

stops.name: Riblah on the Orontes, the forward camp
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Riblah is a recurring headquarters across roughly 604 to 586 BC rather than the site of a datable single event
stops.campa: Riblah is a camp on the Orontes, halfway between Babylon and the coast, and for two decades it is where the west is governed from. Tribute arrives here, judgments are given here, captured kings are brought here. It has no walls worth excavating and leaves almost nothing behind; its whole value is position, close enough to watch Egypt's border and to hold Syria and Phoenicia at once. Second Kings names it again and again as the place where the fate of Judah's kings is settled, far from Jerusalem and far from Babylon both.
suggested_refs: Riblah in the land of Hamath, named repeatedly in 2 Kings 23 and 25

stops.name: Jerusalem, Jehoiakim becomes his servant
stops.date_confidence: traditional; 2 Kings 24:1 gives no year, and the submission is usually placed in 604/603 BC. No Babylonian text names Jerusalem in this window
stops.campa: Jehoiakim, put on Judah's throne by Egypt, becomes the servant of the king of Babylon for three years. There is no siege in the account and no Babylonian tablet names Jerusalem in this window; the tribute is extracted by what happened at Ashkelon rather than by anything done to Jerusalem. Second Kings records the submission in one verse and adds, in the next, that he turned and rebelled. Jeremiah is preaching in the city throughout, telling anyone who will listen that Babylon is the instrument and not the enemy.
stops.quote: And now have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant; and the beasts of the field have I given him also to serve him.
stops.quote_source: Jeremiah 27:6, King James Version. Spoken as the word of the Lord about Nebuchadnezzar, not by him
suggested_refs: Jeremiah's oracles naming Nebuchadnezzar as the servant of the Lord

stops.name: The Egyptian frontier, the battle both armies lose
stops.date_confidence: attested to the regnal year
stops.campa: In the fourth year he marches on Egypt itself. The Chronicle is unusually candid: the two armies meet in open battle and inflict heavy losses on each other, and the king of Akkad turns back to Babylon to refit. It is the only reverse the Chronicle admits in the whole preserved run of the reign. Jehoiakim in Jerusalem reads the withdrawal correctly, as a sign that Babylon can be checked, and stops the tribute. He reads the next three years a great deal less well.
suggested_refs: The Egyptian border fortifications of the eastern Delta under Necho II

stops.name: The Kedarite steppe, the raid on the Arabs
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the place is not attested at all
stops.campa: With Egypt held off and the tribute stopped in Judah, he takes the army into the desert against the Arabs of Kedar, striking camps rather than towns. The Chronicle notes the flocks and the people carried off and moves on. No site can be pinned: the target is tents and herds, and the marker here stands at Dumat al-Jandal, a Kedarite centre of the northern steppe, not at any place the tablet names. Jeremiah preserves an oracle against Kedar and Hazor that is usually read against this campaign.
suggested_refs: Dumat al-Jandal and the Kedarite oases of the northern Arabian steppe

stops.name: Jerusalem, the City of David: the siege of the seventh year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the Chronicle gives 2 Adar of the seventh year, which converts to 16 March 597 BC
stops.campa: Jehoiakim's rebellion brings the army back, and this time it invests the city. He dies during the siege, of what the sources will not agree, and his son Jehoiachin inherits a capital already surrounded. The Chronicle dates the end to the day: the second of Adar in the seventh year. It is the only capture of Jerusalem for which a Babylonian tablet and a biblical chapter can be laid side by side and read against each other. They agree, which is rare enough in this reign to be worth saying plainly.
stops.quote: In the seventh year, the month of Kislimu, the king of Akkad mustered his troops, marched to the Hatti-land, and besieged the city of Judah and on the second day of the month of Addaru he seized the city and captured the king. He appointed there a king of his own choice, received its heavy tribute and sent to Babylon.
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 5 (BM 21946), reverse lines 11'-13', translation as presented on Livius.org after Grayson (1975) and Glassner (2004)
suggested_refs: BM 21946, the Jerusalem Chronicle, British Museum

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount: the first stripping
stops.date_confidence: attested to the campaign; the deportation followed the surrender of 16 March 597
stops.campa: He strips the house Solomon built, the first of two despoilings it will take at his hand. Second Kings lists the gold vessels cut in pieces and carried out with the palace treasury, and ten thousand deported, the artisans and the smiths taken first. Jehoiachin is eighteen years old and has reigned three months and ten days. He goes to Babylon in chains. His uncle Mattaniah is installed and renamed Zedekiah, a client king from his first hour. The Temple itself is left standing, emptied but not burned.
suggested_refs: The Temple Mount, shared pin with the Solomon, Abraham and Cyrus journeys

stops.name: Riblah, Zedekiah installed and sworn
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source places the installation at Riblah
stops.campa: The succession is arranged from the camp on the Orontes rather than in the city. Second Kings says only that the king of Babylon made Mattaniah king in Jehoiachin's place and changed his name; it does not name Riblah, and neither does Ezekiel, who says Zedekiah was bound by oath and broke it. Placing the installation here is inference from what Nebuchadnezzar does at Riblah ten years later, and is offered as inference. No source of either siege puts Nebuchadnezzar himself inside Jerusalem; his officers go up, and he waits on the Orontes.
stops.quote: In the seventh year [of Nebuchadnezzar, 598 BC] in the month Chislev [November/December] the king of Babylon assembled his army, and after he had invaded the land of Hatti (Syria/Palestine) he laid siege to the city of Judah. On the second day of the month of Adar [16 March] he conquered the city and took the king [Jeconiah] prisoner. He installed in his place a king [Zedekiah] of his own choice, and after he had received rich tribute, he sent forth to Babylon.
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Chronicle BM/WA 21946, translation as given in Wikipedia's 'Siege of Jerusalem (597 BC)', citing 'No 24 WA21946, The Babylonian Chronicles, The British Museum'; no translator named, the rendering deriving from D. J. Wiseman, Chronicles of Chaldaean Kings (1956)
suggested_refs: Ezekiel 17, the parable of the two eagles and the broken oath

stops.name: Babylon, the rebellion of the tenth year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: In the tenth year a rebellion breaks out inside Babylon itself, and he puts it down. The Chronicle is terse about it, as it is about everything domestic. The empire's western wars are recorded campaign by campaign; what happens in the capital appears in a clause. Whoever moved against him, and why, and what it cost, are not in the tablet. The gap is a gap: the surviving Babylonian record is a record of armies leaving Babylon, not of the city they leave behind them.
suggested_refs: The Babylonian Chronicle entry for the tenth year, a single clause on internal revolt

stops.name: Babylon, the palace storerooms: rations for Yaukin of Yahud
stops.date_confidence: attested; the tablets carry dates across roughly 595 to 570 BC, and the pin is set at the earliest of them
stops.campa: In the vaulted storerooms under the palace, scribes enter oil rations for Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud, and for his five sons. German excavators find the tablets in the twentieth century, and the Babylonian ledger confirms what the Judean chronicle says from the other side: Jehoiachin lives out his captivity fed at the king's expense, a hostage kept rather than a prisoner punished. A named figure of the Hebrew Bible sits here on a dated administrative tablet, in a ration list, under his Babylonian spelling.
suggested_refs: The Weidner ration tablets, Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin

stops.name: Syria-Palestine, the last entry in the Chronicle
stops.date_confidence: attested; this is the final preserved entry of the series
stops.campa: The eleventh year takes the army west again, and there the Babylonian Chronicle series stops. What survives resumes only near the end of the dynasty. Everything that follows in this journey, the second siege, the burning of the Temple, the years at Tyre, the campaign against Amasis, is known from the Hebrew Bible, from Josephus quoting Berossus, from excavation, and from one broken tablet. The most documented reign of the Neo-Babylonian empire goes dark at exactly the point it becomes famous.
suggested_refs: The break in the Babylonian Chronicle series, 594 to 557 BC

segments.name: The Second Siege and the Burning

stops.name: Jerusalem, the City of David: the siege of the ninth year begins
stops.date_confidence: attested in 2 Kings 25:1 as the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year; that month is rendered here as January, and the year is given as 589 or 588 BC in different reckonings
stops.campa: Zedekiah stops the tribute and gambles on Egypt. The army comes back a third time and rings the city on the tenth day of the tenth month of his ninth year. The siege will run about thirty months, broken once when Pharaoh Hophra marches out and the Babylonians lift off to meet him; Jeremiah tries to leave the city during the interval and is arrested at the gate as a deserter. The lines close again. Lamentations records what the famine inside the walls came to, and does not soften it.
suggested_refs: The Iron Age fortification line of the City of David

stops.name: Lachish, the last signal fire
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the letters and the destruction layer; the ostraca themselves carry no year
stops.campa: While Jerusalem is held, the fortified towns of Judah are reduced one at a time. At Lachish a bundle of ostraca is found in 1935 by James Leslie Starkey's expedition: letters from a junior officer to his commander, ordinary military correspondence, ending mid-sequence. One reports that they are watching for the fire signals of Lachish because they can no longer see Azekah. Jeremiah names Lachish and Azekah as the last two fortified cities still standing. The letters stop; the burnt layer above them continues the account.
suggested_refs: The Lachish Letters, ostraca of the third Wellcome campaign, 1935
sources: Lachish Letters (ostraca), James Leslie Starkey excavation, 1935

stops.name: Riblah, the judgment on Zedekiah
stops.date_confidence: attested to the campaign; the year is given as 587 or 586 BC
stops.campa: The wall is breached and Zedekiah runs for the Jordan. He is overtaken near Jericho and brought north to the camp on the Orontes, where Nebuchadnezzar is waiting. Sentence is given there: his sons are killed in front of him, and that is the last thing he is allowed to see, and then his eyes are put out. He is bound in bronze and taken to Babylon to die. Twice a king of Judah has had his life decided at Riblah. The second verdict is the one the tradition keeps.
suggested_refs: The plain of Jericho, where the flight from Jerusalem was overtaken

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount: Nebuzaradan burns the house
stops.date_confidence: attested, day disputed: 2 Kings 25:8 gives the seventh of Av, Jeremiah 52:12 gives the tenth, and the sources are not reconciled here. The year is given as 587 or 586 BC
stops.campa: A month after the sentence, Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, comes up to Jerusalem and burns the house of the Lord, the king's house, and every great house in the city. The bronze pillars and the bronze sea are broken up for metal and carried east. Four centuries earlier this same courtyard was a seven-year building site filled with cedar and gold and bound labour, raised at Solomon's order as the house of the same god now watching it burn. Consecration at one end of that span, ash at the other.
stops.quote: And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem: And he burnt the house of the Lord, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire.
suggested_refs: The ninth of Av in the Jewish liturgical calendar, which fuses both dated traditions into one fast

stops.name: Jerusalem, the walls pulled down
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the demolition follows the burning within the same campaign
stops.campa: Nebuzaradan's troops pull the walls down, which is a separate decision from taking the city and a slower one. What is left of the population goes east, apart from the poorest, who are left to work the vineyards and the fields. Survey of the Iron Age fortifications shows a demolition horizon rather than battle damage: the stones came down deliberately, course by course. Jerusalem ends the campaign with no wall and no Temple. Neither is rebuilt until the Persian period, a century and a half on.
suggested_refs: The City of David destruction horizon in the Iron Age fortification surveys
sources: Jerusalem excavation reports, via summary literature

stops.name: Mizpah, Gedaliah in the ruined country
stops.date_confidence: disputed: 2 Kings 25:25 puts the murder in the seventh month of the same year, about two months after the appointment, while other reckonings place it in 582/581 BC and tie it to the third deportation of Jeremiah 52:30. Neither is adopted. The identification of Tell en-Nasbeh as Mizpah is itself only probable
stops.campa: He appoints Gedaliah, of a scribal family that had backed Jeremiah, governor over what is left, and seats the administration at Mizpah because the capital is uninhabitable. Gedaliah tells the remnant to farm the land and submit. He is murdered by Ishmael son of Nethaniah, a man of the royal line, and the survivors flee into Egypt against Jeremiah's explicit warning, taking the prophet with them. How long Gedaliah governed the sources do not agree on, and the disagreement is left standing here.
suggested_refs: Tell en-Nasbeh, north of Jerusalem, generally but not certainly identified as Mizpah

segments.name: The Coast, the Cedar, and the Nile

stops.name: Tyre, the siege of the island city
stops.date_confidence: traditional and disputed: only Josephus gives thirteen years, 586 to 573 BC, and he elsewhere dates the siege's start to Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, 598/597, which does not fit his own figure
stops.campa: From Judah he turns north to the Phoenician coast and sits down before Tyre, which is an island, and which his army cannot reach without a fleet it does not have. Ezekiel prophesies the city's fall in detail and then, years later, concedes in a second oracle that the siege earned Nebuchadnezzar no plunder worth what his army spent, every head rubbed bare and every shoulder worn from carrying, wages the god will have to pay him out of Egypt instead. The first oracle is not withdrawn; both stand in the book, one against the other.
suggested_refs: Ezekiel 26 and 29, the two oracles on Tyre that contradict each other
sources: Josephus, Against Apion 1.21, citing Menander of Ephesus

stops.name: Wadi Brisa, the cedar road cut through the mountain
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the rock text carries no year and is dated broadly to the 590s or 580s BC
stops.campa: On a cliff in the cedar country at the northern end of the Bekaa he has a relief and a long inscription cut into living rock. The text describes opening a road through mountains no king before him had opened, to bring cedar down for the temples. He is shown twice: once as builder before the gods, once killing a lion. The timber roofs Esagila and Ezida a thousand kilometres east. Weissbach publishes the reliefs in 1906, by which time the rock face has weathered to the edge of legibility.
suggested_refs: The Wadi Brisa reliefs and inscriptions, published by F. H. Weissbach in 1906

stops.name: Nahr el-Kalb, the ledger of conquerors
stops.date_confidence: undated; the panel carries no legible year and is only broadly placed in the reign
stops.campa: Above the mouth of the Dog River the rock already carries the panels of Ramesses II and Esarhaddon, each conqueror cutting himself into the same cliff on the way past. Nebuchadnezzar adds his own relief and inscription, now weathered nearly to nothing and only partly legible. No year survives on it. His is the last Mesopotamian royal panel the cliff receives; the empires that come afterward cut theirs in Greek, in Latin, in Arabic and in French, and the ledger keeps running into the twentieth century.
suggested_refs: The Nahr el-Kalb commemorative stelae north of Beirut, surveyed by Renan in 1864
sources: Nahr el-Kalb rock inscriptions, comparative epigraphic survey (Renan 1864 and later)

stops.name: Tyre, the terms rather than the storming
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the end date rests on Josephus alone
stops.campa: The siege ends in an arrangement, not a storming. Tyre accepts Babylonian overlordship, Ithobaal III is deposed, and a succession of Babylonian-approved kings and suffetes governs the island afterward. The walls are never breached. Jerusalem, which had land on every side, was razed; Tyre, which had water, was negotiated with. It is the nearest thing to a limit on his western reach that any source records, and the source that records it is Josephus, drawing on Phoenician annals now lost.
suggested_refs: The Phoenician royal annals of Tyre, known only through Menander and Josephus
sources: Josephus, Against Apion 1.21, citing Menander of Ephesus and Phoenician royal annals

stops.name: Migdol, the Egyptian campaign of the thirty-seventh year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the regnal year by BM 33041, whose text breaks where the outcome would be; the location of Migdol is itself disputed and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: In his thirty-seventh year he moves against Amasis in Egypt, and one badly damaged tablet is the whole cuneiform trace of it. The break falls where the outcome would be. It may record a real push into the Delta or a border action that went nowhere. Jeremiah and Ezekiel had both promised this invasion decades before, and Ezekiel had promised it as the wages owed for Tyre. Migdol's own location is disputed among excavators; the pin here is approximate and marks a region, not a findspot.
suggested_refs: BM 33041, the fragmentary Egypt tablet of Nebuchadnezzar's thirty-seventh year

stops.name: Babylon, the throne room of the Southern Palace
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the room is in use across the whole reign and no single date attaches to it
stops.campa: The throne room of the Southern Palace runs more than fifty metres, its facade faced in moulded glazed brick, yellow palmettes and blue columns. Anyone brought before the king walks that whole length first, in view of the court, before he reaches the throne. Tribute is received here and cases are judged here. The Book of Daniel puts the king on the roof above it, looking out over the city and saying the sentence that costs him his reason. The room is real and excavated. The sentence is scripture, and no cuneiform text knows anything about it.
stops.quote: Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
stops.quote_source: Daniel 4:30, King James Version. Words the biblical narrative places in his mouth; their historicity as an utterance is disputed
suggested_refs: The glazed brick throne room facade of the Southern Palace, Koldewey excavation
sources: Koldewey excavation reports, Southern Palace throne room facade

stops.name: Babylon, Etemenanki: the ziggurat of Marduk
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the building inscriptions are undated and the work spans the reign
stops.campa: The ziggurat of Marduk is rebuilt on a scale his own inscriptions say no earlier king matched, bitumen and baked brick raised, in the text's phrase, until its head reaches heaven. Herodotus, in Babylon perhaps a century later, counts eight towers standing one on another. Later tradition folds the structure into the Tower of Babel, and Athanasius Kircher will engrave that tower in his Turris Babel as a spiral going up out of Nimrod's Babylon, two thousand years and a different city away.
suggested_refs: Kircher's Turris Babel (1679), which draws the tower this ziggurat became

stops.name: Babylon, Esagila: the house overlaid in gold
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the building inscriptions are undated
stops.campa: Esagila stands just south of the ziggurat, and of everything he builds it takes the most: the inscriptions describe the sanctuary overlaid in gold until it shines like the sun. Marduk's statue lives here and leaves once a year for the procession, with the king walking as the god's high priest. Gurdjieff will later date the Sarmoung Brotherhood to Babylon and call the line unbroken since, a claim resting on nothing this reign's own inscriptions can confirm. Of the building itself almost nothing survives above the foundations; it was quarried for brick for centuries.
stops.quote: I am Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, the exalted prince, the favourite of the god Marduk, the beloved of the god Nabu, the arbiter, the possessor of wisdom, who reverences their lordship, the untiring governor who is constantly anxious for the maintenance of the shrines of Babylonia and Borsippa, the wise, the pious, the son of Nabopolasser, king of Babylon; To Marduk, my lord I make supplication; Oh eternal prince, lord of all being, guide in a straight path the king whom thou lovest and whose name thou hast proclaimed as was pleasing to thee. I am the prince, the favourite, the creature of thy hand. Thou hast created me and entrusted me with dominion over all people.
stops.quote_source: East India House Inscription, anonymous English translation as given on Wikipedia's East India House Inscription article; the article names no translator and cites no edition for this rendering
suggested_refs: The East India House Inscription, a limestone foundation tablet now in the British Museum
sources: Nebuchadnezzar's Esagila building inscriptions (East India House Inscription)

stops.name: Borsippa, Ezida: the temple of Nabu
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the building inscriptions are undated
stops.campa: At Borsippa, a short way southwest, he rebuilds Ezida, the temple of Nabu, and its ziggurat, in the same devotional formulas he uses at Esagila. Nabu is the god of writing, and once a year he travels by barge to Babylon to join his father Marduk in the procession, so the two cities work as one ritual machine. The ziggurat's summit is fused and blackened, vitrified by heat, and popular tradition has therefore attached the Tower of Babel to Birs Nimrud rather than to Etemenanki, which is where it belongs.
suggested_refs: Birs Nimrud, the vitrified summit of the Borsippa ziggurat

stops.name: Sippar, Ebabbar: the house of Shamash and its archive
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the building inscriptions are undated, though the archive tablets are individually dated
stops.campa: At Sippar he restores Ebabbar, the house of Shamash, a cult older than Babylon's own claim to the south. The building inscriptions are formulaic; the temple archive is not. Sippar has yielded one of the largest cuneiform archives ever recovered, tens of thousands of tablets of grain accounts, loans, rations, priestly rosters and litigation over fields. Read together they give the reign from underneath, in barley issued, wages owed, fields disputed, and the names of the men who kept the count.
suggested_refs: The Sippar archive tablets in the British Museum collection

stops.name: Uruk, Eanna: the priest returns as restorer
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the building inscriptions are undated
stops.campa: He comes back to Eanna as its restorer, sixty years after holding its priesthood. The inscriptions from Uruk use the same devotional template as Babylon and Borsippa and Sippar, piety issued city by city from a single formula. The archives show the temple economy running as it has run for two thousand years, scribes and priests and tenant farmers, an administrative habit older than every dynasty that has claimed it. He restores the house where he learned to write and does not, in the text, mention that he was ever its priest.
suggested_refs: The Eanna precinct at Warka, restored by the king who had been its sanga

stops.name: Babylon, the Babil mound: the North Palace and the gardens that are not in his inscriptions
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the palace is late in the reign, and the garden tradition is unattested in any Babylonian source
stops.campa: Late in the reign a second palace goes up on the Babil mound at the northern edge of the city, and his own inscription claims it was finished in fifteen days. Greek writers, working from Berossus, put the Hanging Gardens somewhere in this complex and explain them as a consolation for a Median queen who missed her mountains. Not one of his inscriptions mentions a garden. Diodorus credits the terraces to an unnamed Syrian king, and one modern argument moves them to Nineveh and Sennacherib altogether.
stops.quote: He erected very high walks, supported by stone pillars, and by planting what was called a pensile paradise, and replenishing it with all sorts of trees, he rendered the prospect an exact resemblance of a mountainous country. This he did to please his queen, because she had been brought up in Media, and was fond of a mountainous situation.
stops.quote_source: Berossus, Babyloniaca, as quoted by Josephus, Against Apion I; William Whiston translation
suggested_refs: Stephanie Dalley, The Mystery of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, which relocates them to Nineveh
sources: Josephus, Against Apion I, citing Berossus

stops.name: Kish, the two cylinders on the ziggurat mound
stops.date_confidence: unverified; the cylinders and their dating could not be checked against the publication
stops.campa: At Kish, on the ziggurat mound east of Babylon, two inscribed clay cylinders of Nebuchadnezzar are said to have been recovered, recording work on the ziggurat there. The report is published in the journal Iraq. That publication was not reachable for this journey, and the two cylinders stand here unverified, entered as a claim with its source named rather than as a fact. Kish itself was ancient before Babylon existed; the Sumerian king list begins the world's kingship here after the flood.
suggested_refs: Tell al-Uhaymir, the mound of Kish, east of Babylon
sources: 'Two Inscribed Cylinders of Nebuchadnezzar II from the Ziggurat of Kish', Iraq (not consulted directly)

stops.name: Babylon, the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way
stops.date_confidence: c. 569 BC in current scholarship; older literature gives c. 575 BC, and the two figures are not reconciled here
stops.campa: The eighth gate of the city is rebuilt in glazed brick the colour of lapis, with striding lions for Ishtar, aurochs for Adad, and mushhushshu dragons for Marduk in registers up the jambs. Behind it runs the Processional Way, down which Marduk's statue is carried each New Year. The dedicatory inscription names the builder. Two and a half centuries later Alexander enters Babylon through this same fabric and sacrifices to Bel-Marduk as the Chaldean priests direct him, passing through a gate this reign watched being fired.
suggested_refs: The Ishtar Gate dedicatory inscription of Nebuchadnezzar

segments.name: The Madness, the Death, and the Long Afterlife

stops.name: Babylon, the fields outside the walls: the seven years of Daniel 4
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated; no Babylonian text records any interruption of the reign, and the Book of Daniel reaches its final form around 167 to 164 BC
stops.campa: The Book of Daniel takes the king out of the palace and puts him in the fields: driven from men, eating grass like an ox, his hair grown like eagles' feathers and his nails like birds' claws, seven years, until his reason is given back and he blesses the Most High. No Babylonian administrative text records any interruption of the reign, and Berossus, who had the temple records in front of him, says nothing of it. Daniel reaches its final form around 165 BC, four hundred years after the king it names.
stops.quote: And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever
suggested_refs: Daniel 4, the first-person confession attributed to the king

stops.name: Babylon, the Southern Palace: death in the forty-third year
stops.date_confidence: attested by the transition of Babylonian regnal date formulas
stops.campa: He dies in the palace he spent forty-three years rebuilding, about eighty years old, at the end of the longest reign the dynasty will have. Amel-Marduk, the Evil-Merodach of Second Kings, succeeds him and in his first year lets the aged Jehoiachin out of prison and seats him at the royal table. Within two years Amel-Marduk is murdered. Twenty-three years after that, Cyrus takes Babylon without a battle and finds the Temple vessels his predecessor carried off still sitting in the treasury.
stops.quote: Nabuchodonosor, after he had begun to build the forementioned wall, fell sick, and departed this life, when he had reigned forty-three years; whereupon his son Evilmerodach obtained the kingdom.
stops.quote_source: Berossus, Babyloniaca, as quoted by Josephus, Against Apion I; William Whiston translation
suggested_refs: Babylonian date formulas marking the accession of Amel-Marduk
sources: Josephus, Against Apion I, citing Berossus

stops.name: Babylon, the grave that is not there
stops.date_confidence: no date; the burial is unlocated and the absence is negative evidence, not proof no tomb existed
stops.campa: No royal tomb of Nebuchadnezzar has been found. No Neo-Babylonian royal necropolis has been located at all, at Babylon or anywhere else, which is a different statement from saying none existed. Koldewey dug the city for eighteen years and turned up palaces, gates, temples, streets and ration tablets, and no king's grave. Alexander will die inside this same palace complex two centuries later, and his body will be fought over for a decade by men who understood exactly what a corpse is worth.
suggested_refs: Koldewey's Babylon excavation records, 1899 to 1917, which locate no royal burial
sources: Archaeological consensus following Koldewey's excavations of Babylon

stops.name: Qumran, the Prayer of Nabonidus
stops.date_confidence: the scroll fragment is dated palaeographically to the first century BC; the tradition it carries is older and undatable
stops.campa: In a cave above the Dead Sea a fragmentary Aramaic scroll turns up telling the story of Daniel 4 about a different king. In it Nabonidus, Babylon's last ruler, is afflicted for seven years at Teima, is healed, and confesses. Nabonidus did spend years away from Babylon; his absence is documented. The likeliest account of the chapter is that the tradition began with him and was later moved onto the far more famous name. The fragment does not prove that. It puts the older version in the ground.
suggested_refs: 4Q242, the Prayer of Nabonidus, Dead Sea Scrolls

stops.name: Berlin, the Pergamon Museum: the gate rebuilt indoors
stops.date_confidence: attested: excavated 1902 to 1914, installed in the Pergamon Museum, which opened in 1930
stops.campa: The gate comes out of the ground in fragments between 1902 and 1914 and is shipped to Berlin, where it is reassembled inside a museum that opens in 1930. What stands there is the smaller frontal gate; the larger rear section, the grander of the two, is in storage and has never been put up. Original glazed brick is combined with new brick fired in a kiln built for the purpose. More people have walked under this gate in Berlin than ever walked under it in Babylon.
suggested_refs: The Museum of the Ancient Near East, Pergamon Museum, Berlin

stops.name: London, the British Museum: the East India House Inscription
stops.date_confidence: attested: found before 1803, registered at the British Museum in 1938 as 1938,0520.1
stops.campa: A limestone tablet covered in ten columns of archaising cuneiform, listing the king's building works across Babylon and Borsippa, is dug up somewhere near Babylon before 1803 by Harford Jones Brydges, then British Resident in Baghdad. It goes to the museum of the East India Company in London, and when those collections are dispersed it reaches the British Museum in 1938. Rawlinson's lithographs put it into print in the middle of the nineteenth century, and the king's own account of himself becomes legible again.
suggested_refs: British Museum registration 1938,0520.1, the East India House Inscription
sources: East India House Inscription provenance record

stops.name: Babylon, the stamped bricks of the reconstruction
stops.date_confidence: 1980s; the individual brick courses are not dated in reachable sources
stops.campa: The Iraqi government rebuilds the walls of the Southern Palace on top of the excavated courses, and the new bricks are stamped with an inscription naming Saddam Hussein as builder in the era of Nebuchadnezzar. It is the oldest gesture in the building: the king had done the same thing himself, stamping his own name into every course he laid over older foundations. Archaeologists objected that the reconstruction destroyed the stratigraphy. In al-Tabari and the Islamic historians after him the king is Bukht-Nasr, who levels Jerusalem and drives its people out of it.
suggested_refs: The Saddam-era inscribed bricks of the Southern Palace reconstruction
sources: Reported accounts of the Saddam-era Babylon reconstruction
